newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FIGURE SKATING-WOTZEL AND STEUER FINALLY TRIUMPH.
newsitem.headline: FIGURE SKATING-WOTZEL AND STEUER FINALLY TRIUMPH.

text.p: German Mandy Woetzel could not land her problem jump, a double axel, but she and Ingo Steuer still won their first world pairs figure skating title on Wednesday.

The Germans, European champions in 1995 and world runners-up in 1993 and last year, had recently called on the services of a psychologist to help them with the aftermath of their failed love affair - and to help Woetzel with the axel.
The doctor was partly successful and their wonderful artistry made up for Woetzel's fall on the axel as they dethroned Russians Marina Eltsova and Andrei Bushkov.
"We are proud of ourselves and we are not surprised to win even with a mistake because we have a very difficult programme," Woetzel said.
"We know if we skate clean we can win and if we make only one mistake we can also win."
Partly explaining the psychologist, she said: "He stops us from getting nervous and helps us be what we are."
Their routine was full of complex lifts, holds and throws.
Eltsova and Bushkov, who added the European title in January, lost their chance of keeping the world crown when Bushkov fell on their opening jump, a triple toe loop.

And when they mounted the podium they were the target of boos by fans who felt the silver medals should have gone instead to former world, Olympic and European champion Artur Dmitriev and his new partner, Oksana Kazakova.
Dmitriev doubled out of an intended triple toe loop for the second night in succession but he and Kazakova still advanced three places to take the bronze medals.
They won the European title last year but were not eligible for this year's event after finishing fourth in the Russian national championships.
They earned their place here by defeating Eltsova and Bushkov in the Champions Series final early this month.
The ruggedly artistic Dmitriev, now 29, probably missed the triple toe loop more in two nights here than in all his years at the top with Natalia Mishkutienok during the early 1990s.
"I never missed it before. Missing my jump was a big shock for us," Dmitriev said.
"When I missed it yesterday I said 'I'm an idiot'. It is too bad because we were really ready for this championship."
Americans Kyoko Ina and Jason Dungjen took fourth place ahead of team mates Jenni Meno and Todd Sand, whom they displaced as U.S. champions last month.

Young Russians Elena Berezhnaia and Anton Sikharulidze, third overnight, had a disastrous finale. He fell on their first two jumps, she fell on the next two throw jumps and they plunged six places to finish ninth.
